title: Effect of Preoperative Vitamin D Deficiency on Hypocalcemia in Patients with Acute Hypoparathyroidism after Thyroidectomy

content: Highlights This meta-analysis evaluated prophylactics for postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia. Teriparatide is the most effective strategy for postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia. Calcium-based supplements are the second most effective strategies. Teriparatide could be a promising alternative for high-risk populations. Postoperative hypocalcemia is a frequent complication following total thyroidectomy, and it exerts additional strain on healthcare resources. The incidence of postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia ranges from 13% to 49%, with 3% of the cases being permanent. A spectrum of clinical manifestations, ranging from mild symptoms such as perioral or acral paresthesia, tingling, and carpopedal tetany to life-threatening complications such as laryngospasm and cardiac arrhythmias, accompany hypocalcemia. The American Thyroid Association recommends administering prophylactic oral calcium and vitamin D to prevent postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia. Routine administration of oral calcium before surgery can reduce postoperative hypocalcemia to ~10%. Since vitamin D is vital for calcium absorption, a combination of calcium plus vitamin D supplementation is proposed for high-risk populations. Recently, teriparatide and perioperative steroids have been shown to reduce the risk of postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia. The relative efficacy and safety of these new alternative strategies compared to routine calcium-based interventions are unclear. An understanding of the comparative efficacy and safety of different hypocalcemia prophylactic strategies is useful for informed clinical decision-making. Three meta-analyses on hypocalcemia prophylaxis have been published, but the results are not conclusive. All of the previous meta-analyses adopted a conventional meta-analysis design and performed a pairwise comparison with a placebo, but the relative efficacy of different strategies was not well-examined. More importantly, additional promising prophylactic strategies have not been evaluated elaborately. In this study, we aim to compare the relative efficacy of different strategies in preventing postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia through systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials (RCTs). This study would provide evidence on two important clinical questions: What are the effective prophylactic strategies for postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia? and Which prophylactic strategy is the most effective? This study has been reported in full adherence to PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) and AMSTAR 2 (Assessing the methodological quality of systematic reviews) guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for publications were searched by two independent authors for information from 1 January 1980 through 1 May 2022. Search strategies were developed using a series of keywords as well as medical subject headings (MeSH) associated with terms relevant to 'thyroidectomy,' 'thyroid surgery,' 'thyroidectomies,' 'hypocalcemia,' 'low calcium,' 'calcium,' 'vitamin D,' 'calcitriol,' 'alfacalcidol,' 'caltrate,' 'cholecalciferol,' ' parathyroid hormone,' 'teriparatide,' 'steroid,' 'dexamethasone,' 'magnesium' together with 'randomized control trial,' with no language restrictions (Supplement 1, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84). Additionally, relevant studies were obtained by reviewing references of relevant meta-analyses and systematic reviews identified in the initial searches. This study was registered on the PROSPERO international prospective register of systematic reviews (CRD42022299982) and Research Registry (reviewregistry1535). The inclusion criteria for the studies considered the: study design (RCT); study populations being adult patients who underwent total thyroidectomy or completion thyroidectomy for benign or malignant thyroid diseases; study intervention whereby patients received one of the following therapies: oral calcium, intravenous calcium, vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol, ergocalciferols, or alfacalcidol), activated vitamin D3 (calcitriol), parathyroid hormone analog (PTH or teriparatide), dexamethasone or magnesium sulfate; study endpoint or outcome measure: either symptomatic hypocalcemia or biochemical hypocalcemia. Studies were excluded if they were: secondary analyses of original RCTs; studies for postoperative pain; active prophylactic treatment combined with other drugs of interest; non-RCTs design; studies published as abstract (hence, insufficient data). A standard data extraction form was used to collect data of interest, as described earlier. The major categories of variables are study characteristics; participant characteristics; type of intervention (type, dose, duration); and outcome characteristics. The percentage of malignant patients, postoperative PTH level, and operating methods of each study were also collected if available. All the above information was extracted independently by two authors, and disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. We used the Cochrane risk of bias assessment tool for randomized trials (RoB 1.0) to examine the methodological quality of included studies. A total of seven domains were examined: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other resources of bias. Each domain was determined as low risk, high risk, or unclear risk. The judgments for each domain are made following the recommendation of the Cochrane Handbook. If there are any disagreements, we resolve them through discussion with a third reviewer. Symptomatic hypocalcemia, defined as the incidence of circumoral tingling and Chvostek and Trousseau signs, as the primary outcomes. Biochemical hypocalcemia, as defined by each individual RCT (e.g., postoperative serum calcium level <8.0 mg/dl) was the secondary outcome. Hypocalcemia cases were calculated per group, and the relative risk (RR) for symptomatic hypocalcemia and biochemical hypocalcemia derived from active prophylactic treatment versus placebo. For multiple treatment groups with different doses of the same drug, data were combined into one treatment group. We first conducted a conventional meta-analysis by comparing any prophylactic treatment with the placebo group. Routine care or nonactive treatment was combined into the placebo group during the evidence synthesis. Heterogeneity was examined using the Q statistics (P<0.05 was considered heterogeneous) and I 2 statistic (I 2>50% was considered heterogeneous). We used comparison-adjusted funnel plots and Egger's test to assess the publication bias. A random-effects model was used to calculate pooled estimates as heterogeneity was anticipated. Both primary and secondary endpoints were estimated as risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals. We then performed a network meta-analysis using a frequentist framework for all study endpoints. We preferred the frequentist over the Bayesian method since the latter can inflate between-comparison heterogeneity when using vague priors in a sparse network. Since heterogeneity is anticipated, we chose the random-effects model as a conservative analysis method to assess the treatment efficacy (RR). Statistical heterogeneity was interpreted using tau 2 (with values <0.04 indicating a low level and tau 2>0.4 a high level) and I 2 statistics (with values of <25%, 25-50%, and >50% representing low, moderate, and high heterogeneity degrees, respectively). When trials contained multiple treatment arms (three or more), inconsistency was defined by the differences between indirect and direct effect estimates for the same comparison. The nod-splitting method examined the consistency between direct and indirect sources of evidence. The surface under the cumulative ranking (SUCRA) was used to rank the efficacy of all prophylactic strategies. For the best treatment, SUCRA is equal to 100%, and for the worst treatment, the value is 0%. We performed two subgroup analyses by restricting studies to only those in which patients received total thyroidectomy and recording efficacy data within 2 weeks. The 95% CIs that did not cross one were considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were conducted using Review Manager 5.3 software (RevMan 5.3, The Cochrane Collaboration, Oxford, UK) and the 'netmeta' package of the R Project for Statistical Computing version 4.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). A total of 1157 citations were identified by literature search. Twenty-seven RCTs and a total of 3382 patients were included for the quantitative analysis (Fig. 1). Eight treatment strategies (oral calcium, intravenous calcium, vitamin D3, activated vitamin D3, oral calcium plus vitamin D3, oral calcium plus activated vitamin D3, teriparatide, dexamethasone, and magnesium sulfate) for postoperative hypocalcemia were evaluated. Comparisons of study characteristics and information therein are shown in Table 1 and Supplement 2, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84. Most patients were female (70.7-85.6%) and in middle age (mean age range: 37-54 years). Over a third (1240, 36.7%) of the patients received thyroidectomy for malignant thyroid tumors, with the rest receiving surgery for benign conditions. The risk of bias in the included trials was assessed by the Cochrane risk of bias tool. There was unclear reporting of randomization sequence in 19% of included RCTs but a low risk of bias for 70% of them. Allocation concealment was at low risk of bias in 19% of RCTs and unclearly reported in 63% of RCTs. Most of the studies were open-labeled trials, and there was a risk of bias from the lack of blinding of patients and clinicians in 69% of RCTs. For studies reporting the primary endpoint, outcome assessors were reported as blinded in 15% of RCTs; incomplete outcome data were reported for 4% of the RCTs. Detailed information on each included RCT is shown in supplements (Supplements 3, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84 and 4, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84). Symptomatic hypocalcemia was examined in 25 trials. Eight placebo-controlled comparisons and four head-to-head comparisons were made, and most of the prophylactic strategies were superior to placebo. Efficacy of oral calcium (five trials), oral calcium plus vitamin D3 (nine trials), and oral calcium plus activated vitamin D3 (five trials) compared to control were the most well-examined. Compared to the placebo, teriparatide had the largest effect size (RR: 0.18; 95% CI: 0.05-0.66), while dexamethasone (RR: 0.49; 95% CI: 0.18-1.36) and magnesium sulfate (RR: 1.20; 95% CI: 0.42-3.41) did not show statistically significant benefits over the placebo. In the head-to-head comparisons, oral calcium plus activated vitamin D3 and oral calcium plus vitamin D3 had similar efficacy (RR: 1.00; 95% CI: 0.41-2.46), but both were superior to oral calcium monotherapy (oral calcium plus vitamin D3 versus oral calcium RR: 0.29; 95% CI: 0.15-0.54) and (oral calcium plus activated vitamin D3 versus oral calcium RR: 0.31; 95% CI: 0.15-0.62). Of the 25 trials included in the symptomatic hypocalcemia network meta-analysis, most studies comprised two arms, with only four RCTs being three arms, and three being four arms. Two studies did not report endpoints for symptomatic hypocalcemia and were thus excluded from the analysis. The network diagram in Figure 2 summarizes the structure of the network formed by interventions, with lines between treatment nodes indicating the direct comparisons made within the included studies. Statistically significant benefits, compared to placebo, were seen with teriparatide (RR: 0.18; 95% CI: 0.03-0.98), oral calcium plus vitamin D3 (RR: 0.43; 95% CI: 0.26-0.71), and oral calcium plus activated vitamin D3 (RR: 0.42; 95% CI: 0.25-0.73). Magnesium sulfate did not reduce the risk of symptomatic hypocalcemia, while other treatments failed to show significant benefits (Fig. 3). Pairwise comparisons are shown in Table 2, while ranking based on SUCRA is given in Supplement 5, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84. Teriparatide displayed the highest probability of being the best treatment (SUCRA=88%). A moderate level of heterogeneity was seen among trials (I 2=65%), with direct and indirect comparisons featuring eight treatment pairs. Only the oral calcium versus oral calcium plus vitamin D3 pair showed significant evidence of inconsistency (P=0.016) (Supplement 6, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84). The proportions of direct evidence for each network estimate were high when compared to the placebo, while the proportion of direct evidence for estimates between two active pairs was low, suggesting that evidence on these pairwise comparisons was insufficient (Supplement 7, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84). Sensitivity analysis involving the inclusion of only total thyroidectomy studies (excluding seven trials) or studies with efficacy data within 2 weeks (excluding four trials) did not reveal any substantial changes to the estimates (Supplements 8, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84 and 9, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84). Publication bias was examined with comparison-adjusted funnel plots and Egger's test suggested there would be potential publication bias for symptomatic hypocalcemia (P=0.0012) (Supplement 10, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84). Fifteen trials involving the eight prophylactic strategies mentioned earlier were examined (12, 14, 15, 17-19, 30, 31, 33, 36, 37, 39, 40, 42, 43). Seven placebo-controlled comparisons and two head-to-head comparisons were conducted. While the efficacy of oral calcium plus vitamin D3 (six trials) compared to placebo was the most well-examined, no trials examined the efficacy of dexamethasone and magnesium sulfate. Several treatments were superior to placebo with teriparatide displaying the greatest effect (RR: 0.27; 95% CI: 0.10-0.76). Monotherapy with plain (RR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.57-1.15) or activated (RR: 0.57; 95% CI: 0.31-1.06) vitamin D3 did not show significant benefits. Of the 15 trials included in the biochemical hypocalcemia network meta-analysis, two RCTs were three-arm studies, and two were four-arm studies, whereas all others were two-arm studies. Study features and the relative risk of each treatment compared with the placebo are presented in Table 1. Observations were similar to those obtained using conventional meta-analysis (Fig. 3). Pairwise comparisons and ranking based on SUCRA (Supplement 5, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84) were also conducted. Intravenous calcium (SUCRA=90%) and teriparatide (SUCRA=88%) outperformed oral calcium plus vitamin D3 (SUCRA=60%). A moderate level of heterogeneity (I 2=23.9%) was evident among trials, and no inconsistencies were apparent (Supplements 11, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84 and 12, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84). Publication bias was examined with comparison-adjusted funnel plots and Egger's test suggested there would be potential publication bias (P=0.0279) for biochemical hypocalcemia (Supplement 13, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/A84). In this study, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first network meta-analysis of RCTs which, directly or indirectly, compare prophylactic strategies for postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia. Besides the commonly used strategies (calcium and vitamin D3), we evaluated teriparatide, dexamethasone, and magnesium sulfate, which are underexamined in previous studies. The major findings of this study are that teriparatide is a promising prophylactic strategy for hypocalcemia, showing the largest efficacy for symptomatic hypocalcemia than all other strategies, and that combination therapy of oral calcium plus either vitamin D3 or activated vitamin D3 are effective strategies for postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia. Monotherapy involving either oral calcium or vitamin D3 appears effective but much less so compared to combination therapy of oral calcium plus vitamin D3. The 2020 American Thyroid Association guideline recommends various strategies to prevent postoperative symptomatic hypocalcemia following total thyroidectomy. Routine prophylaxis using oral calcium and/or vitamin D supplementation for all thyroidectomy patients has been proposed. However, a lack of empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of these strategies has hampered implementation. A previous meta-analysis including 15 randomized controlled studies showed that routine administration of oral calcium and vitamin D could be effective prophylactic interventions as these reduced the risk of symptomatic hypocalcemia (risk difference (RD): -0.25: 95% CI: -0.32 to -0.18) and biochemical hypocalcemia (RD: -0.24; 95% CI: -0.31 to -0.17) compared to a strategy based on measurement of calcium levels. Recently, additional prophylactic strategies using different medications such as teriparatide, steroid, and magnesium offer promising alternatives. However, the relative efficacy of the established calcium-based supplement versus other pharmaceuticals has not been well-examined. In the current meta-analysis, we evaluated the relative efficacy of available prophylactic strategies for hypocalcemia. Teriparatide had the highest efficacy in reducing symptomatic hypocalcemia, followed by oral calcium plus activated vitamin D3, and oral calcium plus vitamin D3. Monotherapy using oral calcium, intravenous calcium, vitamin D3, and dexamethasone, although offering some improvements, did not attain a statistically significant threshold. As with previous traditional meta-analyses, we find combination therapies (oral calcium plus vitamin D3 or oral calcium plus activated vitamin D3) to be effective for symptomatic hypocalcemia. Monotherapy of oral calcium or intravenous calcium is effective for biochemical hypocalcemia and could be effective for symptomatic hypocalcemia, as the indirect meta-analysis might have reduced study power than the direct meta-analysis. Furthermore, monotherapy using vitamin D3 or activated vitamin D3 did not reduce either symptomatic or biochemical hypocalcemia, suggesting that vitamin D3 or activated vitamin D3 should not be used alone. Leveraging on a network meta-analysis design, we examined the relative efficacy of various strategies and found teriparatide to have the highest probability of offering the best outcomes. Recently, a RCT showed that teriparatide (subcutaneous infusion twice daily) improved symptoms of hypocalcemia within 24 h in patients with symptomatic hypocalcemia following thyroidectomy. Therefore, teriparatide could be an alternative pharmacologic intervention for postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia refractory to first-line calcium and vitamin D3 therapy. As previously reported, nearly 3% of hypocalcemia cases, primarily caused by bilateral parathyroid ligand damage or insufficient blood supply, are permanent. While the incidence of permanent hypocalcemia is rare, the consequences are devastating and can dramatically reduce the quality of life. To prevent permanent hypocalcemia, meticulous dissection during surgery is crucial. A thyroidectomy performed by an experienced surgeon can lower the incidence of permanent hypoparathyroidism to 2%. Studies have shown that labeling techniques like carbon nanoparticles, intraoperative indocyanine green, and near-infrared autofluorescence can reduce transient hypoparathyroidism and inadvertent parathyroid resection. As hypocalcemia in patients with permanent hypoparathyroidism is caused by long-term PTH insufficiency, teriparatide replacement therapy can, theoretically, be effective. Use of teriparatide, however, is limited by its high cost, and it is therefore rather reserved as a last resort in permanent hypoparathyroidism and cases refractory to routine therapy. The major strength of this study is in the network design that we adopted, providing an efficacy ranking of different prophylactic strategies for hypocalcemia. There are, however, some limitations to the current work. First, this analysis includes a relatively small number of RCTs for some treatment strategies, especially for noncalcium-based interventions. Second, we did not analyze the safety of different strategies because of the lack of safety data for most included trials. Third, we focused on transient hypocalcemia, but the length of study follow-up varied across RCTs (from 1 day to 30 days). Results from sensitivity analyses restricted to studies with follow-up length within 2 weeks did not reveal any substantial changes in the results, suggesting that heterogeneity in the follow-up might not be resulting in bias. Fourth, some patient characteristics, especially postoperative PTH level and central lymph node dissection, were important risk factors for postoperative hypocalcemia. Patients who received total thyroidectomy and central lymph node dissection, or have postoperative PTH decline, would be more likely to experience postoperative hypocalcemia. However, this information was not always available for study-level meta-analysis. As such, future individual patient-level meta-analysis may help provide a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of postoperative PTH level and central lymph node dissection on postoperative hypocalcemia and develop an individualized prophylactic strategy. Fifth, most RCTs were open-labeled trials, which might lead to additional bias in reporting the primary endpoint of symptomatic hypocalcemia. Since symptomatic hypocalcemia is a subjective endpoint and could possibly be biased in an open-label setting, we examined laboratory hypocalcemia as the secondary endpoint. Results of laboratory hypocalcemia and symptomatic hypocalcemia were highly consistent, suggesting the determination of symptomatic hypocalcemia is reliable.

title: Relative efficacy of prophylactic strategies for postthyroidectomy hypocalcemia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis

content: Autosomal dominant hypocalcemia (ADH) is a disorder of systemic calcium homeostasis that is associated with enhanced sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) to extracellular calcium (Ca2+ o) concentrations.(1-3) The CaSR is a guanine-nucleotide binding protein (G-protein)-coupled receptor (GPCR) that plays a pivotal role in Ca2+ o homeostasis by transducing increases in the prevailing Ca2+ o concentration into multiple signaling cascades that include Gq/11-protein-mediated activation of phospholipase C (PLC), which in the parathyroid glands and kidneys induces rapid increases in intracellular calcium (Ca2+ i) that lead to decreased parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion and increased urinary calcium excretion, respectively.2, 4, 5 ADH is a genetically heterogeneous disorder most commonly caused by germline gain-of-function mutations of the CaSR, which is encoded by the CASR gene on chromosome 3q21.1, and this is referred to as ADH type 1 (ADH1; OMIM #601198).1, 2, 5 However, some ADH patients and families have recently been shown to harbor germline mutations of G-protein subunit-alpha11 (Galpha11), which is encoded by the GNA11 gene (Fig. 1) on chromosome 19p13.3,3, 6, 7 and referred to as ADH type 2 (ADH2; OMIM #615361).3 These ADH-associated Galpha11 mutations have been demonstrated to enhance CaSR-mediated signaling in cellular studies, consistent with a gain-of-function.3, 7 ADH1 patients have calcitropic phenotypes, such as hypocalcemia with inappropriately low or normal PTH concentrations and a relative hypercalciuria that is characterized by urinary calcium to creatinine ratios that are within or above the reference range,1, 8, 9 and mice with a gain-of-function CaSR mutation, that are representative of ADH1, have been reported to also have non-calcitropic phenotypes such as cataracts.10 Although these features are similar to hypoparathyroidism, ADH1 is considered to represent a distinct disease entity from hypoparathyroidism, because affected individuals generally have PTH concentrations that are detectable and within the reference range.1, 8 Furthermore, ADH1 patients may also develop a Bartter-like syndrome characterized by hypokalemic alkalosis, renal salt wasting, and hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism,11, 12 and the use of active vitamin D metabolites to treat symptomatic ADH1 patients may result in the development of marked hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, and renal impairment.1, 9 In contrast to ADH1, the phenotypic spectrum of ADH2 has not been fully elucidated, especially because only five ADH2 probands with Galpha11 mutations (Fig. 1) have been reported to date.3, 6, 7 Thus, it remains to be established whether ADH2 patients with germline gain-of-function Galpha11 mutations are susceptible to hypercalciuria, particularly when treated with active vitamin D preparations, or at risk of a Bartter-like syndrome. Moreover, Galpha11 is a widely expressed protein that mediates the biological effects of GPCRs in a range of tissues,13 and it is currently unknown whether patients with ADH2 may harbor additional calcitropic and non-calcitropic phenotypes. We ascertained a family with ADH and keratoconus, a non-calcitropic disorder of the cornea, and hypothesized that either a single genetic abnormality may be causing ADH and keratoconus, or that ADH and keratoconus may be due to two different genetic abnormalities; ie, digenic inheritance. To explore these hypotheses, we undertook whole-exome sequencing (WES) analysis of two relatives, both of whom had hypocalcemia, and one of whom also had keratoconus, to identify the causative variant(s). The proband (individual I.4; Fig. 2 A) is a 66-year-old male, from Iran, who was diagnosed with hypocalcemia at the age of 16 years following a childhood history of intermittent muscle cramps. His serum adjusted-calcium concentrations have ranged from 1.82 to 1.95 mmol/L (normal range = 2.20 to 2.60 mmol/L), in association with mild hyperphosphatemia (serum phosphate = 1.42 to 1.81 mmol/L; normal range = 0.80 to 1.45 mmol/L), normal serum creatinine concentrations of 72 to 80 micromol/L (normal range = 44 to 133 micromol/L), low/normal serum PTH concentrations of 4.0 to 18.7 pg/mL (normal range = 12 to 65 pg/mL), a normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration of 18.7 ng/mL (normal range = 10 to 50 ng/mL), and a normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D concentration of 25.7 pg/mL (normal range = 16 to 45 pg/mL). He had been treated with oral calcium and active vitamin D preparations, and developed non-obstructive bilateral nephrolithiasis in association with urinary calcium values ranging from 4.3 to 10.2 mmol/24 hours (normal range = 2.5 to 7.5 mmol/24 hours). He was found to have mild bilateral cataracts at the age of 62 years. His family history revealed that 11 relatives (7 males and 4 females) over three generations had hypocalcemia, with symptoms such as seizures, muscle cramps, and tetany. Affected relatives also had low circulating PTH concentrations, and relative or absolute hypercalciuria (Fig. 2 A), and these findings supported a diagnosis of ADH. Five hypocalcemic family members (3 males and 2 females) and one normocalcemic family member also had keratoconus, a corneal disorder, which in individuals II.3, II.5, and II.7 (Fig. 2 A) had developed between the ages of 30 and 34 years.14 There was no consanguinity and the inheritance of hypocalcemia from father to son in individuals; eg, from I.1 to II.1 and II.2; I.4 to II.5; and II.5 to III.1 (Fig. 2 A), indicated that hypocalcemia was transmitted as an autosomal dominant disorder. Similarly, the inheritance of keratoconus from father to son in individuals II.5 to III.1 (Fig. 2 A), may be because keratoconus is transmitted as an autosomal dominant disorder, but the occurrence of keratoconus in the children (II.3, II.5 and II.7; and II.8) of unaffected parents (I.4 and I.5; and I.8 and I.9, respectively, Fig. 2 A) indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance or autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance. To investigate the cause of the hypocalcemia and keratoconus in this family, venous blood samples were collected from four available patients, of whom two had hypocalcemia only (individuals I.4 and II.4), and two others had both hypocalcemia and keratoconus (individuals II.3 and II.5; Fig. 2 A). Leukocyte DNA was extracted using the Gentra PureGene blood kit (Qiagen, Crawley, UK). CaSR mutations, which would cause ADH1, and mutations of three genes, GCMB, PTH, and AIRE1, which are known to cause hypoparathyroidism had been previously excluded by an accredited genetics diagnostic laboratory. Informed consent was obtained from all participants included in the study, using protocols approved by the UK Multicentre Research Ethics Committee (MREC/02/2/93) and the Hospital Research Ethics in Israel. Exome capture was performed in individual I.4, who was affected with hypocalcemia, and in individual II.5, who was affected with both hypocalcemia and keratoconus (Fig. 2 A), using the SeqCap EZ Human Exome Library v2.0 (Roche NimbleGen, Madison, WI, USA),15 and DNA sequences determined using a 100-bp paired-end read protocol on an Illumina HiSeq2000 platform.15 A minimum of 20x vertical read depth was obtained for >88% of the coding exome, as specified by the consensus coding sequence (CCDS) project,16 in both individuals. Reads were aligned to the Human Sequence version 37d5 (hs37d5) reference genome using Stampy17 and variant calling of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and short insertions and deletions (indels) was undertaken using Platypus (v0.5.1).18 Analysis of coding variants was undertaken using Ingenuity Variant Analysis. To search for variants causing hypocalcemia and keratoconus under autosomal dominant inheritance models, variants with a minor allele frequency (MAF) >5% within all populations of 100 genomes data (April 2012 phase 1 call set [v3 update]) and from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) exome sequencing project (Exome Variant Server, NHLBI GO Exome Sequencing Project (ESP), Seattle, WA (http://evs.gs.washington.edu/EVS/), were excluded. To search for variants causing keratoconus under an autosomal recessive inheritance model, variants with a MAF >5% were not excluded. The pathogenicity of variants was inferred from several criteria: allele frequency within the NHLBI exome sequencing project and the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC) (Cambridge, MA, USA; http://exac.broadinstitute.org/), amino acid conservation, physicochemical alterations in amino acid substitutions, splice site prediction algorithms (NNSPLICE [http://www.fruitfly.org/seq_tools/splice.html], MaxEntScan [http://genes.mit.edu/burgelab/maxent/Xmaxentscan_scoreseq.html], GeneSplicer [http://www.cbcb.umd.edu/software/GeneSplicer/gene_spl.shtml], and SpliceSiteFinder-Like [http://www.interactive-biosoftware.com]), and literature review. Variants of interest were confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Sanger DNA sequence analysis of the appropriate exons, using leukocyte DNA samples from the four available family members and two unrelated unaffected individuals, as reported.19  Amino acid sequences of Galpha-subunit paralogs and transforming growth factor, beta-induced (TGFBI) orthologs were aligned using the Clustal Omega program (European Bioinformatics Institute, the European Molecular Biology Laboratory). The crystal structure of Galphaq in complex with the GTP analogue guanosine diphosphate (GDP)-AIF4 has been determined (Protein Data Bank [PDB] accession number 3OHM),20 and this was used to model Galpha11, which has 90% identity with Galphaq at the amino acid level, using the PyMOL Molecular Graphics System (version 1.2r3pre; Schrodinger, LLC). The generation of wild-type and mutant Leu341 pBI-CMV2-GNA11 expression constructs have been reported.3 Site-directed mutagenesis was used to generate the Val to Met mutation at codon 340 in the pBI-CMV2-GNA11 construct using the Quikchange Lightning Site-directed Mutagenesis kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) and gene-specific primers (SigmaAldrich, St Louis, MO, USA), as reported.19 For all studies, empty vector, wild-type, or mutant pBI-CMV2-GNA11 expression constructs were transiently transfected into human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 cells stably expressing the CaSR (HEK293-CaSR) using Lipofectamine 2000 (LifeTechnologies, Carlsbad, CA, USA).21 Cells were maintained in DMEM-Glutamax media (ThermoFisher, Waltham, MA, USA) with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and 400 mug/mL geneticin (ThermoFisher) at 37 C, 5% CO2. Successful transfection was confirmed by visualizing GFP fluorescence using an Eclipse E400 fluorescence microscope with a Y-FL Epifluorescence attachment and a triband 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole-FITC-Rhodamine filter, and images captured using a DXM1200C digital camera and NIS Elements software (Nikon).3, 21, 22 The expression of Galpha11, GFP, calnexin, and CaSR proteins was also determined by Western blot analysis using anti-Galpha11 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA), anti-GFP (Santa Cruz), anti-calnexin (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA), or anti-CaSR (Abcam, Cambridge, UK) antibodies. The Western blots were visualized using Immuno-Star WesternC kit (BioRad, Hercules, CA, USA) on a BioRad Chemidoc XRS+ system.3  The Ca2+ i responses of HEK293-CaSR cells expressing wild-type or mutant Galpha11 proteins were assessed by a flow cytometry-based assay, as reported.2, 3, 21, 22 In brief, HEK293-CaSR cells were plated in T75 flasks and transiently transfected 24 hours later with 16 mug DNA.3 At 48 hours posttransfection, cells were detached, resuspended in calcium (Ca2+)-free and magnesium (Mg2+)-free Hanks buffered saline solution (HBSS) and loaded with 1 mug/mL Indo-1-acetoxymethylester (Indo-1-AM) for 1 hour at 37 C. After removal of free dye, the cells were resuspended in Ca2+-free and Mg2+-free HBSS and maintained at 37 C. Transfected cells, in suspension, were analyzed by flow cytometry on a MoFlo modular flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN, USA) and data on the Ca2+ i responses to alterations in Ca2+ o collected from all cells that expressed GFP, by simultaneous measurements of GFP expression (at 525 nm), Ca2+ i-bound Indo-1AM (at 410 nm), and free Indo-1AM (ie, not bound to Ca2+ i) (at 485 nm), using a JDSU Xcyte laser (Coherent Radiation, Santa Clara, CA, USA), on each cell at each Ca2+ o concentration [Ca2+]o, as described.3, 21 Assays were performed in four biological replicates for each of the expression constructs. The peak mean fluorescence ratio of the transient response after each individual stimulus was measured using Cytomation Summit software (Beckman Coulter), and expressed as a normalized response, as described.3, 21 Nonlinear regression of concentration-response curves was performed with GraphPad Prism using the normalized response at each [Ca2+]o for each separate experiment for the determination of the EC50 (ie, [Ca2+]o required for 50% of the maximal response). Data is presented as mean with confidence interval or mean +- standard error of the mean (SE). Statistical analysis was performed using the F-test. A value of p < 0.05 was considered significant for all analyses. Exome capture and high-throughput sequence analysis of genomic DNA from two affected individuals, one with hypocalcemia (individual I.4) and the other with hypocalcemia and keratoconus (individual II.5) (Fig. 2 A) resulted in the detection of >5000 non-dbSNP variants in both individuals. The exclusion of variants with a MAF of >5% resulted in the identification of 104 novel variants in 103 genes, of which three variants were excluded as sequence artifacts as they occurred within trinucleotide repeats. The only variant identified in a gene previously associated with hypocalcemia, was a heterozygous G>A transition at nucleotide c.1018 (c.1018G>A), located in exon 7 of the GNA11 gene (Fig. 1). The variant was confirmed by Sanger DNA sequencing to be present in both patients affected with hypocalcemia (individuals I.4 and II.5) and in two other family members (individuals II.3 and II.4) with hypocalcemia from whom samples were available (Fig. 2 B). This G>A transition (GTG to ATG) resulted in a missense substitution, Val340Met, of the encoded Galpha11 protein (Fig. 2 C). The absence of this DNA sequence abnormality in >60,000 exomes from the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC), together with evolutionary conservation of the Val340 residue in vertebrate Galpha-subunit paralogs (Fig. 3 A) indicated that the Val340Met abnormality likely represented a pathogenic GNA11 mutation rather than a benign polymorphic variant. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a novel heterozygous c.1209T>G transversion in TGFBI, encoding a variant His403Gln in TGFBI, which was present in both individuals (I.4 and II.5, Supporting Fig. 1 A, Supporting Table  1). The TGFBI His403Gln variant is not present in ExAC, although a different variant in the same amino acid, His403Tyr, is present in only 3 out of >60,000 individuals. The His403 residue is also evolutionarily conserved in TGFBI orthologs (Supporting Fig. 1 B). The TGFBI variant was confirmed by Sanger DNA sequence analysis in the siblings, II.3 and II.5, who had hypocalcemia and keratoconus, but its absence in the sister II.4, who has hypocalcemia only, indicates that this TGFBI variant is not involved in the etiology of hypocalcemia (Supporting Fig. 1 A). Moreover, the presence of this TGFBI variant in the father (individual I.4), who was affected with hypocalcemia only, indicates likely nonpenetrance of the mutant allele (Supporting Fig.  1A). To evaluate whether the Val340Met GNA11 variant represents a pathogenic mutation and the cause of hypocalcemia in this family, structural and functional studies were undertaken. The crystal structure of Galphaq, which shares 90% amino acid identity with Galpha11,3, 20 was used to predict the effects of the Val340Met mutation. The mutated Val340 residue is located within the alpha5 helix of the GTPase domain of Galpha11 (Fig. 3 B, C), and next to the Phe341 residue, which has been reported to be associated with a gain-of-function Phe341Leu mutation (Figs. 1 and 3B) causing ADH2.3 The alpha5 helix is located at the C-terminus of Galpha-subunits and plays a critical role in GPCR binding and G-protein activation.23, 24 Indeed, the C-terminal portion of the alpha5 helix, which is known as the interface module, directly binds to the transmembrane domain and intracellular loops of activated GPCRs,24 whereas the N-terminal portion, which is known as the transmission module, interacts with the GTPase domain beta-sheet, comprising the beta1-beta6 strands (Fig. 3 C), to mediate conformational changes in Galpha-subunit structure that facilitate guanine nucleotide exchange.23, 25 The Val340 residue is predicted to form non-polar interactions with the conserved Phe272 and His327 residues, located in the beta5 and beta6 strands, respectively (Fig. 3 C), which are considered to stabilize the binding of G-protein with ligand-bound GPCR.23, 25, 26 The Val340Met mutation is predicted to impair the interaction with the His327 Galpha11 residue (Fig. 3 D), thereby altering the conformation of the alpha5 helix and/or beta6 strand, and destabilizing the Galpha-GPCR complex. To determine the effects of these predicted changes in Galpha11 structure (Fig. 3) on CaSR-mediated signaling, bidirectional pBI-CMV2-GNA11 expression constructs containing wild-type Val340, mutant Met340, or the previously reported gain-of-function Leu341 mutant GNA11 cDNA,3 or vector containing the GFP reporter gene alone were transiently transfected into HEK293 cells stably expressing the CaSR. Expression of CaSR, Galpha11, and GFP was confirmed by fluorescence microscopy and/or Western blot analysis (Fig. 4 A, B). Calnexin was used as a loading control in Western blot analyses, and Galpha11 expression was demonstrated to be similar in cells transiently transfected with wild-type or mutant Galpha11 proteins, and greater than that of cells transfected with the empty pBI-CMV2 vector (Fig. 4 B). The responses of [Ca2+]i to alterations in [Ca2+]o in cells expressing the different GNA11 vectors were assessed by flow cytometry. The Ca2+ i responses in wild-type and mutant Galpha11-expressing cells were shown to increase in a dose-dependent manner following stimulation with increasing concentrations of Ca2+ o between 0 and 15 mM. However, expression of the Met340 and Leu341 mutant Galpha11 proteins resulted in a leftward shift of the concentration-response curves (Fig. 4 C), with significantly lower half maximal (EC50) values, compared to wild-type Val340 Galpha11 and empty vector (Met340 = 2.44 mM [95% CI, 2.31 to 2.77 mM]; Val340 = 3.14 mM [95% CI. 3.03 to 3.26 mM]; empty vector = 3.12 mM [95% CI, 2.99 to 3.25 mM]; p < 0.0001) (Fig. 4 D). There was no significant difference in the EC50 values between Met340 and Leu341 (Leu341 = 2.60 mM; 95% CI, 2.49 to 2.72 mM; p > 0.05). Thus, the Val340Met missense substitution represents a novel gain-of-function Galpha11 mutation, similar to those reported in ADH2 patients.3, 7  The identification of a germline gain-of-function Galpha11 mutation, Val340Met, indicates ADH2 to be the likely cause of hypocalcemia in this family. To date, five other hypocalcemic patients and families have been reported to harbor germline Galpha11 mutations, consistent with a diagnosis of ADH2.3, 6, 7 Similar to the family characterized in this study, individuals with germline gain-of-function Galpha11 mutations have been reported to generally have mild-to-moderate hypocalcemia (serum adjusted-calcium concentrations ranging from 1.75 to 2.15 mmol/L) in association with serum PTH concentrations that are detectable and within the lower half of the normal range.3, 6, 7 However, despite ADH2 being associated with mild biochemical features, affected individuals are commonly symptomatic and may present with paresthesia, muscle cramps, carpo-pedal spasms, or seizures.3, 6, 7 Moreover, as described for the proband in this study (individual I.4, Fig. 2 A), some ADH2 patients appear susceptible to treatment-related hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, and nephrolithiasis,7 although affected individuals likely have a milder urinary phenotype, with significantly reduced urinary calcium excretion compared to ADH1 patients who harbor gain-of-function CaSR mutations.7 Furthermore, patients with germline heterozygous gain-of-function Galpha11 mutations, in contrast to patients with germline heterozygous gain-of-function CaSR mutations, may have non-calcitropic phenotypes. For example, short stature caused by postnatal growth insufficiency was reported in affected individuals from a multigenerational kindred with hypocalcemia and a germline heterozygous gain-of-function mutation, Arg60Leu,7 and it is possible that the occurrence of mild bilateral cataracts in the proband (individual I.4) may also be due to the germline gain-of-function Galpha11 mutation, Val340Met. It is also of interest to note that somatic Galpha11 mutations that lead to constitutive G-protein activation are associated with the development of uveal melanomas.27 However, keratoconus, a corneal disorder, was not observed in all patients harboring the germline Val340Met Galpha11 mutation, thereby indicating that keratoconus is not due to the Galpha11 mutation. Instead, keratoconus in this family is likely due to the identified novel germline variant, His403Gln in TGFBI (Supporting Fig. 1), abnormalities of which have previously been reported in association with keratoconus and autosomal dominant forms of corneal dystrophy.28, 29 Thus, the occurrence of keratoconus and ADH2 in this family are not genetically associated, but are instead due to digenic inheritance of mutations involving TGFBI and Galpha11. Structural and functional studies of ADH2-causing gain-of-function Galpha11 mutations have revealed residues and peptide motifs critical for Galpha-subunit function. Thus, the importance of the interface at which the Galpha-subunit helical and GTPase domains interact to mediate guanine nucleotide exchange, has been demonstrated by the reported Arg60Leu, Arg60Cys, and Arg181Gln Galpha11 mutations,3, 6, 7 which are located at the interdomain interface (Fig. 3 B), 25 and predicted to disrupt GDP binding.3, 6, 7 Whereas, the reported ADH2-causing Ser211Trp mutation, located in the alpha2 helix of the GTPase domain (Fig. 3 B), may cause a gain-of-function by dissociating the Galpha-subunit from the Gbetagamma heterodimer.6 Furthermore, the reported ADH2-causing Phe341Leu mutation3 is located in the C-terminal alpha5 helix, which facilitates G-protein-GPCR coupling,23 and the mutated Phe341 residue is predicted to play major roles in G-protein activation and inactivation.25, 26 Indeed, under basal conditions, Phe341 forms part of a hydrophobic cluster of phenylalanine residues that maintains the Galpha-subunit in an inactive GDP-bound conformation.25, 26 Upon ligand-binding, Phe341 binds to the second intracellular loop of the activated cognate GPCR,24 which disrupts the hydrophobic cluster, leading to the release of GDP.25, 26 The Phe341Leu mutation is predicted to affect the hydrophobic cluster,3 thereby leading to GDP/GTP exchange and G-protein activation. In contrast to these roles of Phe341, the neighboring Val340 residue does not bind to activated GPCRs and is not involved in GDP/GTP exchange,24, 25 but instead may play a role in stabilizing the nucleotide-free conformation of the Galpha-subunit once bound to activated GPCR.23 Thus, the Val340Met mutation likely mediates Galpha11 activation by influencing the stability of Galpha-GPCR interactions. These different ADH2 mutations have yielded insights into Galpha-subunit structure-function relationships, which may aid the design of novel targeted therapeutic agents for the treatment of ADH, for which there is currently a lack of adequate drugs.30  In conclusion, we have identified a novel germline gain-of-function Galpha11 mutation, Val340Met, that causes ADH2 in a family in which some members also suffered from keratoconus. Keratoconus in this family was likely due to a novel germline TGFBI His403Gln variant, thereby indicating that keratoconus and ADH2 are not caused by the same mutation, but instead the combined occurrence of ADH2 and keratoconus in some family members is due to digenic inheritance. Finally, our study provides an exemplar of the clinical utility of WES, that enabled the identification of two likely genetic causes by a single experimental protocol, which would not have been readily possible using former genetic techniques.
